context.title: SF YIMBY — November 3, 2026 California general election endorsements

subject.title: Governor of California

positions.statement: We support Xavier Becerra because of the commitment he made when he filled out our questionnaire: "I will pursue legislation to ensure state housing law applies in the coastal zone just like everywhere else."

subject.title: Attorney General of California

positions.statement: YIMBY Action endorses Rob Bonta for Attorney General because he has been one of the strongest enforcers of California's housing laws. In 2021 he created the Housing Strike Force, the first unit in the AG's office dedicated to holding cities accountable for breaking state housing law. Since then his office has taken on cities that tried to dodge their obligations, from suing Huntington Beach to stopping Woodside's attempt to block new homes by declaring itself mountain lion habitat. Just this summer, he warned Menlo Park that it can't use legal loopholes to stall a major housing project. Pro-housing laws only matter if someone enforces them, and Bonta has shown he will.

subject.title: San Francisco Board of Supervisors, District 6

positions.statement: Looking forward, Supervisor Dorsey is excited about the advancement of state bill AB 2074, which would streamline high-rise residential construction near regional transit hubs. He would like to work on local analogues to the fee transparency and predictability reforms that YIMBY has pushed at the state level and further streamline ADU approvals. On the state's 25,000-unit rezoning mandate, he would like to continue to upzone transit-rich corridors like The Hub, Van Ness, and Market Street, while ensuring that west-side neighborhoods finally carry their fair share. SF YIMBY endorses Matt Dorsey to continue to champion the housing legislations and reforms that the city needs.

subject.title: San Francisco Board of Supervisors, District 8

positions.statement: SF YIMBY is endorsing Gary McCoy in the top slot due to his history of commitment to YIMBYism and his strong potential as a member of the board of supervisors. McCoy has been a public ally in our fight for more housing for a decade, and has a great focus in his policy goals towards things that make housing of all kinds easier to build. His vision along with his political savvy will help San Francisco build more of the housing we desperately need.

subject.title: San Francisco Board of Supervisors, District 10

positions.statement: SF YIMBY endorses Theo Ellington for District 10 supervisor. We support the commitments he made in his SF YIMBY questionnaire: six-story single-stair buildings, more homes near transit, objective by-right approvals, project shot clocks, and consequences when review deadlines are missed.

subject.title: San Francisco Assessor-Recorder

positions.statement: Joaquin Torres is running unopposed for another term as Assessor-Recorder, and SF YIMBY is happy to endorse him again. While this office's core job — fairly assessing the city's roughly $350 billion in taxable property and maintaining public records — isn't a land-use lever, Torres has built a long track record as a reliable pro-housing official.

subject.title: BART Board of Directors, District 8

positions.statement: SF YIMBY is proud to endorse Sara Barz for Bart Board District 8. Sara has years of experience in transportation and supports more housing in the Bay Area. She is a co-founder of Seamless Bay Area, an organization dedicated to making transit fares more integrated across the region. Her technical experience has enabled mobile payments for public transportation around the world. Housing needs transportation and transportation needs dense housing. Sara has the vision to support BART and housing in both the nearterm and longterm. She supports building more housing near BART stations (transit oriented development) which would help both BART’s ridership recovery and address our housing crisis. As part of her long-term vision, she supports planning for more rail transit on the West side of San Francisco, enabling more connectivity in an area recently upzoned by the City. SF YIMBY endorses Sara as someone with the technical knowledge to fill the role and as someone who understands the need for better housing and public transportation in the Bay Area.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition A (Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions)

positions.statement: Proposition A is a collection of various technical fixes to the City’s charter. For the planned merger of the Department of Building Inspections and the Planning Department to be successful, the Building Inspection Commission (which oversees the Department of Building Inspection) will need to be updated as well. SF YIMBY endorses Proposition A because it gives the Board the flexibility to make those updates instead of requiring yet another ballot measure.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition C (Contributions to the Housing Fund)

positions.statement: Prop C raises the city's annual contribution to the Housing Trust Fund, which pays for subsidized housing construction, preservation, and downpayment assistance. The contribution climbs from about $51M today to $125M a year by the late 2020s, tied to growth in general fund revenue or property values, whichever is faster. The best thing about the Housing Trust Fund is that it doesn't tax new homes out of existence, but instead aligns the revenue incentives of the city to promote new growth. The measure also lets the Board pause or trim contributions in bad budget years, so it isn't a blank check. SF YIMBY is proud to endorse the single most consequential affordable housing-supply fix on this November’s ballot.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition D (Changes to Ballot Measure Process)

positions.statement: This isn't abstract governance trivia for YIMBYs. San Francisco's rock-bottom signature threshold is exactly how a small, well-funded opposition group can lock in an anti-housing rule that the elected Board can never fix without another citywide vote. Raising the bar to put something on the ballot, and making it require an actual Board majority to route around normal legislating, cuts down on that vector for freezing bad housing and zoning policy into the Charter. Shorter ballots, more accountable lawmaking.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition E (City Administrator's Authority and Changes to City Contracting)

positions.statement: Prop E centralizes city purchasing rules under the City Administrator instead of leaving them scattered across a hundred-plus code sections that nobody owns and nobody can fix. It's the same dysfunction that gave the city its infamous $1.7M toilet, and it's also the dysfunction that slows down every park, playground, and public infrastructure project the city needs, including the public realm work adjacent to housing growth. When a 2024 reform simplified small-project purchasing, Rec and Park renewed the Bernal Heights Playground for $1.3M in about a year, instead of the years and multiples of the cost that comparable projects took under the old rules. Housing supply doesn't happen in a vacuum — it needs functioning city infrastructure processes around it, and Prop E is a real fix.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition F (Changes to Executive Branch Management)

positions.statement: The city's mazelike permitting process for housing persists as a perennial contributor to our housing shortage. Mayor Daniel Lurie seeks to simplify housing approvals as part of his PermitSF campaign, by combining the Planning Department with the Department of Building Inspections. Unifying these two important departments will create a new optimized pathway to build more housing. Enacting this reform requires voters to pass Proposition F, which cleans up the City Charter so Mayor Lurie and future mayors can streamline and reorganize city departments. SF YIMBY endorses a vote of YES to fix a long-broken system that worsens our housing shortage.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition G (Allowing Private Vehicles on the Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park)

positions.statement: In the 2024 General Election, San Franciscans voted to create a large, permanent, oceanfront park where the Great Highway once was, to make a more liveable and enjoyable city for all of us to call home. Since April 12, 2025, the 2-mile oceanfront park has been used every day of the year, averaging 4,900 daily visits (3,800 on weekdays, 7,200 on weekend days and holidays). Former Supervisor Mar has publicly changed his opinion in favor of the park, having seen the impact firsthand. SF YIMBY is proud to continue to support this park and endorses voting NO to closing the park and bringing back the highway.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition H (Parcel Tax to Fund Public Muni Operations)

positions.statement: Transit and housing supply are the same fight. Every unit of housing in this city only works if people can actually get around. SF YIMBY is proud to support this measure.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition I (Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax)

positions.statement: "Prop I: Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax · San Francisco, CA · Vote no" … "While spending more on subsidized affordable housing and social housing are worthy goals, the transfer taxes which fund Prop I will reduce the overall housing supply and drive up rents. San Francisco has the highest property transfer taxes in the state (California’s base rate is 0.11% vs San Francisco’s up to 6%), adding roughly $30,000 to the cost of every new home according to a 2020 report from the city controller. While this proposition marginally reduces the transfer tax, it simultaneously removes the ability to make additional reductions to get it down to zero. Proposition I ties the hands of the Board of Supervisors, never allowing them to lower it without going to the ballot. This makes no sense when the city controller has said that the tax should be eliminated entirely. Taxing housing in order to build housing is self-defeating."

subject.title: Bay Area — Regional Measure RTM (Regional Transit Measure)

positions.statement: The Regional Transit Measure is the regional Connect Bay Area sales tax across five counties, funding Muni, BART, Caltrain, and the smaller regional operators. The regional nature of the BART necessitates a financial backstop that has united 3 county governments in this effort. BART has already cut over a billion dollars in costs since 2019 and without new revenue, it may face a 63% cut in train hours, three lines instead of five, 9pm closures, and fare hikes of up to 50% starting in 2027, followed by station closures and mass layoffs. A regional economy this large cannot function with a gutted BART, and a modest, sunsetting sales tax is a far better outcome than losing the system.
